drafted_from: tool:renew-a-tls-certificate's row in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/tool-rows.json, do-work/renew-a-tls-certificate.mjs, do-work/tls-host-owner.py and the tests in test/
start_here: Say to your AI: "Dry-run the certificate renewal for app.example.com on my server at 192.0.2.34 as admin with its pinned key." It runs tool:renew-a-tls-certificate with dryRun true, asks the staging authority, and tells you whether the DNS records stayed as they were.
no_lists_because: It keeps no list of its own: it takes one server's facts as its input and answers what that server's certificate owner reports.
instructions: 1. Gather the server's facts: its public name, IPv4 address, SSH port, the administrator you sign in as, its pinned key ("<address> ssh-ed25519 <key>") and its layout (host: owner path, state folder, downloads folder, ingress, receptionist). The README in tools/renew-a-tls-certificate/ shows a made-up one.

2. Say to your AI the sentence in start_here. It calls run_resource_operation at @workshop-tools with method tools:run, tool tool:renew-a-tls-certificate and that input (the worked example shows one). The door mounts your server administration key for the run; you paste no key.

3. Read what comes back: the certificate as the server verified it (hostname, certificate_present, system_trust_and_hostname_verified, not_before_local, not_after_local, issuer, serial, private_key_mode) plus preexisting_dns_records_unchanged, certificate_changed and dry_run. An {"error": ...} or a thrown message names what to change (for example the layout or the pinned key was refused).

4. Run it once with dryRun true to prove the key and the DNS permission work, then declare a wake for tool:renew-a-tls-certificate every 6 hours (every_ms 21600000) with the same input and no dryRun, so the address stays renewed.
